prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Poetry? It’s a hobby. I run model trains. Mr Shaw there breeds pigeons. It’s not work. You dont sweat. Nobody pays for it. You could advertise soap. Art, that’s opera; or repertory— The Desert Song. Nancy was in the chorus. But to ask for twelve pounds a week— married, aren’t you?— you’ve got a nerve. How could I look a bus conductor in the face if I paid you twelve pounds? Who says it’s poetry, anyhow? My ten year old can do it and rhyme. I get three thousand and expenses, a car, vouchers, but I’m an accountant. They do what I tell them, my company. What do you do? Nasty little words, nasty long words, it’s unhealthy. I want to wash when I meet a poet. They’re Reds, addicts, all delinquents. What you write is rot. Mr Hines says so, and he’s a schoolteacher, he ought to know. Go and find work.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Poetry, Shaw, You

outputs.L1: Poetry? It’s a hobby. I run model trains; Mr. Shaw there breeds pigeons. It isn’t work. You don’t sweat. Nobody pays for it. You could advertise soap. Art—that’s opera, or repertory: *The Desert Song*. Nancy was in the chorus. But to ask for twelve pounds a week—married, aren’t you?—you’ve got a nerve. How could I look a bus conductor in the face if I paid you twelve pounds? Who says it’s poetry, anyway? My ten-year-old can do it and rhyme. I get three thousand and expenses, a car, vouchers—but I’m an accountant. They do what I tell them, my company. What do you do? Nasty little words, nasty long words—it’s unhealthy. outputs.L2:
Poetry? That’s just something you do in your spare time. I operate miniature railways; Mr Shaw over there keeps pigeons. It isn’t a proper job. There’s no hard labour in it, and no one pays you for it. You might as well be writing adverts for soap. Real art is opera, or repertory theatre—something like *The Desert Song*. Nancy used to sing in the chorus.

But expecting twelve pounds a week—especially when you’re married, aren’t you?—that takes some cheek. How could I justify paying you twelve pounds when a bus conductor has to earn his money? And who decided it counts as poetry in the first place? My ten-year-old can write verses, and he even makes them rhyme.

I earn three thousand a year, with expenses, a company car, and vouchers, but then I’m an accountant. In my firm, people do as I say. What exactly do you contribute? A few unpleasant short words, a few ugly long ones—it’s not wholesome. Whenever I meet a poet, I feel like scrubbing myself clean. They’re all left-wingers, drug users, troublemakers. What you produce is rubbish. Mr Hines says the same, and since he’s a schoolteacher, he should know. Go and get a real job.
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents a dismissive and hostile view of poetry, treating it not as a serious profession but as a casual pastime or hobby. Rather than recognizing poetry as legitimate creative labor, the speaker implies that it is something a person might do privately in their spare time, without deserving payment or public support.

This attitude is reinforced through comparisons between poetry and other activities or forms of art. The speaker suggests that poetry is less useful, less impressive, or less valuable than other kinds of work and artistic production. By placing poetry below more practical occupations and even other creative pursuits, the speaker frames it as an indulgence rather than a meaningful contribution to society.

A central argument made by the speaker concerns money. The speaker insists that paying a poet twelve pounds a week would be impossible to justify, especially when ordinary workers earn their wages through difficult, practical labor. From this perspective, supporting a poet financially would seem unfair, wasteful, or even insulting to people who perform more conventional kinds of work.

The speaker’s criticism also becomes personal and prejudiced. Poets are portrayed with contempt and suspicion, as if they are unhealthy, irresponsible, delinquent, or politically dangerous. Instead of engaging seriously with the value of poetry, the speaker attacks the character of poets themselves, suggesting that they are not respectable members of society.

Ultimately, the speaker concludes that poetry has no real worth. By dismissing it as useless and telling the poet to find “real work,” the speaker reduces artistic creation to something inferior to paid manual or practical labor. The overall tone is scornful, revealing a narrow view of value in which only conventional employment is considered legitimate.
outputs.L4:
The text takes the form of a satirical monologue in which an accountant speaks with open contempt about poetry and those who write it. Through this speaker’s voice, the piece exposes a narrow, materialistic view of the world: only work that produces a clear wage, a measurable profit, or a socially approved status is treated as valuable. The accountant judges poets not by the insight, beauty, or emotional truth their work may offer, but by their lack of conventional employment, their uncertain income, and their failure to fit into respectable professional life.

This attitude reveals a broader social prejudice against artistic labor. Poetry is dismissed as useless because it does not appear to serve an immediate practical purpose. The poet is treated as idle or irresponsible, while the accountant’s own values—order, money, calculation, and respectability—are presented as the standards by which all human activity should be measured. The satire lies in the fact that the accountant’s certainty exposes his limitations. His contempt for poetry shows not wisdom, but an inability to understand forms of value that cannot be entered into a ledger.

By giving voice to this judgmental and practical-minded speaker, the text criticizes a society that reduces human worth to productivity and income. It suggests that when art is evaluated only in terms of wages or conventional success, its deeper importance is ignored. Poetry may not produce material wealth in an obvious way, but it contributes to culture, imagination, emotional understanding, and the expression of human experience. The monologue therefore becomes more than a simple attack on one accountant’s opinion; it is a critique of a wider social tendency to undervalue creativity and to treat artists as less serious or less useful than those in traditional professions.

Ultimately, the text highlights the conflict between artistic value and material value. It shows how easily creative work can be dismissed when society recognizes only what is profitable, practical, or respectable. Through satire, the piece invites readers to question such assumptions and to recognize that poetry and art possess forms of meaning that cannot be measured by money alone.
outputs.L5:
Poetry has a way of turning ordinary moments into something unforgettable. It gives shape to feelings we often struggle to explain, using rhythm, image, and silence as much as words. In poetry, a single line can hold a memory, a question, or an entire world.

George Bernard Shaw, though best known as a playwright and critic, understood the power of language deeply. His writing often challenged society, questioned tradition, and pushed people to think more clearly about themselves and the world around them. Like poetry, Shaw’s work reminds us that words are not just decoration—they can provoke, inspire, and transform.

And then there is you, the reader. Poetry is never complete until someone receives it. Your thoughts, experiences, and emotions give each poem new life. A poem may have been written long ago, but when you read it, it becomes present again. It speaks differently to every person, and that is part of its beauty.

Poetry, Shaw, and you are connected by the power of expression. Whether through verse, drama, or personal reflection, language invites us to see more deeply and live more thoughtfully.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical dramatic monologue in the voice of a smug middle-class accountant dismissing a poet who has asked to be paid twelve pounds a week.
counterfactuals.output:
Twelve pounds a week?

My dear young man, let us be serious.  
I am as fond of literature as anyone—  
there is a very handsome edition of *The Golden Treasury*  
in our front room, between the clock and the aspidistra—  
but twelve pounds a week is not a sentiment,  
it is an item.

You must learn to distinguish between the two.

Now, I have listened with patience, I think,  
to your remarks about “vision,”  
and “the necessity of song,”  
and “the wounds of the age,”  
which no doubt are all very moving  
when arranged in irregular lines.  
But here, in this office,  
the wounds of the age must be entered in ink,  
under the proper heading,  
and supported, where possible, by receipts.

Twelve pounds a week!  
For poems?

I do not wish to be vulgar,  
but one must ask what a poem does.  
A clerk files.  
A porter carries.  
A typist types.  
A salesman, at least in theory, sells.  
Even a curate can be said to perform  
some vague but socially acknowledged function  
among the elderly and the dying.

But a poet?  
You tell me he “bears witness.”  
To what, precisely?  
The weather?  
His childhood?  
The moon’s effect upon his nerves?  
We have newspapers for the first,  
families for the second,  
and doctors, if necessary, for the third.

Please do not misunderstand me.  
I am not unsympathetic.  
I have myself, on occasion, felt things.  
There was a morning last March, for instance,  
when the fog over the golf course  
struck me as quite unusually suggestive.  
But I did not invoice anybody for it.

That is the difference between us.

You say the nation must support its artists.  
The nation, my dear fellow,  
is already supporting a great many persons  
who have stronger claims on its purse:  
widows, pensioners, civil servants,  
and, not least, those of us  
whose sober calculations prevent the entire edifice  
from collapsing into lyricism.

Imagine the precedent.  
Today twelve pounds for a poet;  
tomorrow a sculptor wants coal allowance  
because marble is cold;  
then some young woman with cropped hair  
demands a stipend to “explore silence.”  
Before long the country is bankrupt,  
and no one has balanced anything  
except perhaps a metaphor.

Besides, hardship is traditional, is it not?  
I was always given to understand  
that poets thrive on garrets, rejection,  
and a certain attractive pallor.  
Pay them properly and what happens?  
Comfort. Regular meals. Dental appointments.  
The Muse, I suspect, would pack her bags at once  
and move in with a starving violinist.

No, no. You must not deprive yourself  
of the very privations  
on which your profession so handsomely depends.

Twelve pounds a week would spoil you.

It would make you prudent.  
Respectable, even.  
You might begin to save.  
You might purchase a hat.  
You might marry, insure your life,  
and develop opinions about drainage.  
And then where would the poems be?

My advice is this:  
take a small post somewhere—teaching, perhaps,  
or cataloguing, or assisting an uncle in trade—  
something regular, something with hours.  
Write your verses in the evenings,  
as other men do crossword puzzles  
or cultivate dahlias.  
If they are good, posterity will reward you;  
if they are bad, no harm has been done.

Posterity, I may add,  
is famously economical.  
It pays in plaques.

As for the twelve pounds,  
I cannot recommend it.  
The figure is excessive,  
the purpose obscure,  
and the return on investment  
almost impossible to calculate.  
One cannot enter “beauty” in a ledger.  
One cannot depreciate “truth.”  
One cannot audit “rapture,”  
though I have known several partners who would try.

So let us be sensible.  
Here is a small honorarium—  
not payment, you understand;  
that would imply a service rendered—  
but a token of encouragement.  
Enough, perhaps, for a pair of shoes,  
or several weeks of tobacco,  
depending on how intensely you intend to suffer.

And when next you feel compelled  
to address the eternal,  
do remember:  
the eternal has no payroll department.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short prose-poem where an employer angrily explains why poetry is not “real work,” comparing it to hobbies like model trains and pigeon breeding.
counterfactuals.output:
“Poetry?” the employer barked, slapping the desk as if it owed him rent. “Poetry is not real work. Real work arrives at eight, sweats through its shirt, fills out forms, moves inventory, answers phones, makes something you can stack, ship, invoice. Poetry is what men do in basements beside model trains, polishing tiny engines that never deliver freight. Poetry is pigeon breeding—cooing over useless feathers, naming birds that only circle back to the same roof. Don’t hand me a page of moonlight and call it labor. Don’t tell me you were busy listening to rain. Rain has never met a deadline. A metaphor never kept the lights on.”

Outside his window, the pigeons lifted like scattered ash. Somewhere, a miniature train went on circling its perfect, unprofitable world.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a bitter, comic anti-arts rant from the perspective of a philistine businessman who thinks poets are lazy, immoral, and overpaid.
counterfactuals.output:
Let me tell you what’s wrong with this country: poets.

There, I said it. While the rest of us are up at dawn moving units, optimizing margins, and bravely attending breakfast meetings in windowless hotel conference rooms, poets are lying in bed “observing the light.” Observing the light! I observe the light every morning too, usually as it flickers over the spreadsheet that determines whether forty-seven people get dental.

And what do poets contribute? They take perfectly serviceable words—words with jobs, words that used to mean things like “invoice,” “shipment,” and “overdue”—and they send them wandering around in little gangs, unemployed, wearing scarves. Then they call it a “collection.” I have collections too: receivables, parking tickets, stress-related prescriptions. Mine are useful.

Poets are forever complaining about being misunderstood. Of course they’re misunderstood. They spend twelve pages comparing loneliness to a spoon. A spoon! If one of my salesmen came in and told me the fourth quarter was “a blue animal breathing under the floorboards,” I’d have security escort him out and make him pay for the coffee.

And don’t get me started on their work ethic. A businessman works sixty hours a week and is called “aggressive.” A poet stares out a window for six months, writes “the moon is a wound,” and suddenly there’s a grant application. Overpaid? Don’t laugh. I’ve seen these people get checks for “residencies,” which apparently means living somewhere nice while failing to answer email. I had a residency once. It was called a lease, and it came with penalties.

They say poetry is necessary for the soul. Wonderful. Is the soul net-30? Can the soul be amortized? Does the soul accept ACH transfers? I have asked my accountant about the soul, and he says it is not deductible unless used exclusively for business purposes.

And immoral? Absolutely. Not in the fun, efficient way—no offshore accounts, no tasteful bribery, no golf-course understandings. No, their immorality is worse: they make poverty look decorative. They sit in cafés, owing everyone money, scribbling about “desire” while occupying a table for four hours on one espresso. A decent capitalist, at least, has the courtesy to be greedy in bulk.

Poets also have a suspicious relationship with time. They’re always “between projects.” I know what I call an employee who is between projects: available for termination. But poets say it with pride, as if unemployment were a delicate migratory bird. “I’m waiting for the language to arrive,” they say. Try telling that to a client. “Sorry, Mr. Henderson, the language has not arrived, but when it does, it will be devastating.”

And the readings! Have you been to one? A room full of adults nodding gravely while someone whispers about rain. Nobody laughs, nobody claps at the right time, and at the end they sell little books for twenty dollars that contain less print than a shampoo bottle. At least a shampoo bottle gives instructions.

No, I say shut it down. Replace poetry departments with small appliance repair. Turn literary festivals into trade shows for dependable shelving. Let metaphors find honest work in advertising, where they belong. If people need beauty, sell it to them by subscription with three pricing tiers and a free trial.

The poets will protest, naturally. They’ll write manifestos. They’ll gather under banners that say things like “The Unmarketable Must Live.” Fine. Let them live. But let them live in the real world, where the rent is literal, the coffee costs money, and if you want to compare your heartbreak to a field of burning horses, you’d better be prepared to monetize the horses.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a 1950s/1960s British-style monologue in which a respectable office manager refuses to fund a poet, using class prejudice and absurd comparisons.
counterfactuals.output:
Now look here, Mr. Pemberton, I’ve given the matter every consideration, and when I say “every consideration” I mean I’ve considered it twice: once before luncheon, when I was charitable, and once after luncheon, when I was sane.

You come into my office — a perfectly respectable office, with ledgers, invoices, and a calendar from the Midland Bank — and you ask me to finance poetry. Poetry, Mr. Pemberton. Not a fleet of vans, not a new duplicating machine, not even a modest improvement to the staff lavatory, which at least would have a measurable return. No. You want capital for feelings.

I have nothing against poetry in its proper place. A few lines on a tombstone, perhaps, or on a Christmas card from an aunt with too much time and no dependants. But as a going concern? As an investment? One might as well underwrite a cloud, or insure a sigh, or put a down payment on a particularly wistful puddle.

You say you are “a voice of the age.” Well, that may be so. But I have met the age, Mr. Pemberton, and it does not pay promptly. The age has been in arrears since 1919 and is still arguing with the cashier.

And let us be frank. You are not, if I may put it delicately, quite our sort of client. I don’t mean that unkindly. I mean it accurately. Your shoes are expressive, your hair has opinions, and your collar appears to have seceded from the rest of your shirt. In this firm, a man’s collar should not be making political gestures.

You tell me you live in a room above a tobacconist and subsist chiefly on cigarettes and revelation. That may be very suitable for the Continent, but in England we prefer a man to have breakfast. A poet without breakfast is not a visionary; he is a nuisance with cheekbones.

No, no, don’t protest. I’ve heard your sample verses. “The moon is a broken saucer in the sink of night.” Very vivid, I’m sure. But if one of my junior clerks came to me describing crockery in that condition, I should ask who was responsible and deduct it from wages. That is the difference between commerce and art: commerce knows who broke the saucer.

You suggest that posterity will thank me. Posterity, Mr. Pemberton, has never once settled an account. I cannot take a letter from posterity to the bank manager and say, “There you are, Mr. Wilkins — eternal gratitude at three and a half per cent.” He would have me removed, and quite right too.

Besides, I have responsibilities. There are salaries to pay, stamps to buy, carbon paper to replenish. Miss Frobisher in accounts has been with us twenty-three years, and I cannot look her in the eye and say, “Your Christmas bonus has become a sonnet sequence about fog.” She would take it badly. Women of that generation often do.

You mention Shelley. They always do. Shelley, Keats, Blake — all very well now they’re safely dead and bound in calf. But I put it to you: would you have lent Blake five pounds on a Tuesday? A man claiming to see angels in Peckham? Not without security, you wouldn’t. And even then you’d want a guarantor.

The trouble with poets is that they mistake rejection for persecution and punctuality for fascism. You arrive forty minutes late, call it “resistance to mechanical time,” and expect me to applaud. If my typist resisted mechanical time, Mr. Pemberton, the post would not go out.

No. I am not funding your little magazine, your pamphlet, your reading series, or whatever it is you call four young men in scarves frightening a kettle in a basement. I shall not pay for ink to be arranged in such a way that ordinary people feel they have failed to understand rain.

Go and get a position. Something steady. Insurance, perhaps. Warehousing. There is dignity in warehousing. A warehouse may not rhyme, but it stands up in weather.

And if you absolutely must write poems, do so in the evenings, quietly, after supper, like a vice with a fountain pen. That is how civilised men manage their disturbances.

Good day, Mr. Pemberton. And mind the umbrella stand on your way out. It is modern, but at least it serves a purpose.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a caustic speech by a conservative accountant telling a poet to get a proper job, mentioning soap adverts, bus conductors, schoolteachers, and “Reds.”
counterfactuals.output:
My dear fellow, I have looked over your “calling,” as you insist on calling it, and I can only say that if inspiration were taxable, even the Revenue would send it back marked “insufficient substance.”

Poetry! A splendid occupation for a man with no rent to pay, no dependants to feed, and no acquaintance whatsoever with the price of coal. You sit there manufacturing sighs about the moon while honest people are manufacturing invoices, ledgers, soap adverts, bus tickets, and lesson plans. Yes, soap adverts! Laugh if you like, but at least they persuade somebody to buy something useful. A bar of soap has done more for civilisation than a hundred thin volumes of verse about alienation.

Why not become a bus conductor? There’s poetry enough in getting people from one place to another, and you’d learn the rare art of making change—something your present profession seems determined to avoid. Or be a schoolteacher, if they’ll have you: stand before a class and discover how little the world is improved by sensitive young men muttering about clouds. At least schoolteachers are underpaid in a respectable way.

But no, you prefer to drift about with your hair and your principles, denouncing “materialism” from cafés whose bills you cannot settle. And I suppose, when the arithmetic becomes too cruel, you’ll blame capitalism, society, bankers, fathers, and the usual Reds’ hymnbook of excuses. Always someone else’s fault that the poet has no shoes—never the poet’s fault for trying to pay the cobbler in metaphors.

Get a proper job. Put on a collar. Learn a trade. Balance a column. Sell soap, clip tickets, teach fractions—anything with a wage, a timetable, and some measurable benefit to mankind. Then, if after a day’s honest work you still feel compelled to write sonnets, do so privately, quietly, and at your own expense, like any other minor vice.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
